name: glibc (libc string functions, qsort, regexec, strtod, malloc)
baseline: musl libc (the copy bundled with zig 0.15.2, statically linked)
workload: 32 libc micro-benchmarks (benchmark.c), each calibrated to a target run time and reported as ns per call: strncmp, strcpy, strncpy, strstr, strchr, qsort of 4096 ints, regexec of an e-mail pattern over 128 lines, strtod over 256 numbers, malloc/free small and medium, printf family, file I/O, and others.
claimed_speedup: glibc fastest in 17 of 32 rows (musl 2, musl+jemalloc 11, 2 ties); README summary: 'glibc wins most benchmarks'. ns/op, glibc vs musl: strncmp 9.91 vs 366.91; strcpy 22.05 vs 129.35; strncpy 25.20 vs 136.77; strstr_search 36.28 vs 104.23; strtod_parse 52.40 vs 226.72 (4.3x, derived from page data); regex_match 117.54 vs 694.23 (5.9x, derived from page data); qsort_int 214387.15 vs 591408.11 (2.8x, derived from page data); malloc_free_small 10.78 vs 122.61; malloc_free_medium 828.38 vs 3343.75. musl is faster on atoi_parse 3.96 vs 9.28, bsearch_int 10.52 vs 16.02, strtok_parse, strrchr 157.31 vs 354.19 and memcpy 154.19 vs 4043.27; musl+jemalloc beats glibc malloc_free_medium 80.59 vs 828.38.
compiler_and_flags: zig 0.15.2 (zig cc, clang 20.1.2); -std=c11 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto=full -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math -g0 -s; targets x86_64-linux-gnu and x86_64-linux-musl (run.sh)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U with Radeon Graphics; Linux 6.8.0-87-generic (Ubuntu 22.04 kernel); run 2025-11-18
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars (unofficial bminor/glibc mirror); the default libc of most Linux distributions
tradeoffs: LGPL: the normal route is dynamic linking, static linking brings LGPL obligations and breaks NSS and iconv loading. Much larger runtime than musl. The comparison is for x86-64 on one CPU; glibc's speed on str*/mem* routines depends on per-CPU variant selection (general knowledge, not shown on the benchmark page). malloc is the default ptmalloc2 and loses to jemalloc on the medium-size row.
caveats: Third-party hobby repo (7 stars, 7 commits, no licence file shown), one machine, one calibrated run per benchmark with no repeats or variance. glibc version is not stated: the binary is built with zig cc -target x86_64-linux-gnu and runs against the host's own glibc (host looks like Ubuntu 22.04, so probably 2.35, an inference). The musl side is compiled by zig from its bundled musl source (version and zig's libc optimisation level not stated) and linked statically, while glibc is the distro's prebuilt dynamic library, so the two sides are built differently. Several rows are not meaningful: strlen, strcmp and memcmp show about 0.1 ns/op (pure calls hoisted out of the loop, ties), the memcpy row has glibc 26x slower than musl (4043.27 vs 154.19, looks like a harness artifact), and the strstr haystack is cut to about 16 KB because the strcpy that plants the first marker writes a NUL (read from benchmark.c). A second vendor blog (BellSoft Alpaquita, which sells a musl build with tuned routines) reports glibc ahead of musl on memcpy and memcmp; the page was EGRESS_BLOCKED here and its numbers are not used. repo_url is the read-only mirror (archived 2026-02-15, last commit 2026-01-20); upstream development continues at sourceware.org, which was not opened. Baseline is a C library, not a C++ standard library.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill (seed-record pass): started from the listed page https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/ (EGRESS_BLOCKED); WebSearch 'libc-bench glibc musl results memcpy malloc pthread_create regex time seconds benchmark repository' (github.com, gitlab.com, git.musl-libc.org filter) surfaced fereidani/musl-vs-glibc

name: GLM (glm::mat4 add and multiply)
baseline: Eigen (Matrix4f, 2011 snapshot eigen-eigen-13a11181fc5a); CML 1.0.2 also measured
workload: Element-wise addition and multiplication of lists of 4x4 float matrices (10 matrices per call, call repeated 1,000,000 times per cell, so 10M matrix operations per cell), wall time with gettimeofday, on a 2011 MacBook Pro and a stock HTC Desire phone.
claimed_speedup: Android HTC Desire, milliseconds, lower is better. armeabi-v7a: GLM additions 1506 vs Eigen 2181 (1.45x, derived from page data), multiplications 2189 vs 5143 (2.35x, derived from page data). armeabi-v7a with NEON: additions 1407 vs 2145 (1.52x, derived from page data), multiplications 3108 vs 5113 (1.65x, derived from page data). Author: 'GLM is the fastest on the HTC Desire with both ABIs' (plain armeabi is a tie: additions 10256 vs 9944, multiplications 59008 vs 59460). Opposite result on the SSE x86 build: Eigen additions 30 vs GLM 76, multiplications 86 vs 400.
compiler_and_flags: GCC, version not stated. CMakeLists Release flags -g0 -O2 (README: all tests -O2 except the non-SSE laptop build, which is -O0); x86 build adds -msse2 -msse3 -mssse3 -msse4.1 -msse4.2 -fopenmp; Android builds (NDK android-9 platform) add -mfloat-abi=softfp -mfpu=neon.
hardware: i7 2.2 GHz early-2011 MacBook Pro (Mac OS X Lion); stock HTC Desire (Android 2.2) with a 1 GHz Qualcomm QSD8250
tradeoffs: Header-only, GLSL-style API; SIMD paths are opt-in through GLM_FORCE_* configuration and aligned types; no expression templates or lazy evaluation, so chained operations create temporaries. GLM is a graphics-oriented library and not a general linear-algebra package.
caveats: Weak and old evidence: a single hobbyist repo (42 stars, 15 commits, no licence shown) from 2011-2012 that vendors GLM 0.9.3.B, CML 1.0.2 and an Eigen 3 snapshot; current GLM 1.0.3 and Eigen 3.4+ behave differently. Only 4x4 float add and multiply were measured. On the tested Intel CPU with SSE, Eigen is 2.5x (additions) and 4.7x (multiplications) faster than GLM, and the author chose Eigen for that reason. The GLM win is on 2010 phone ARM cores (armeabi-v7a) and the plain armeabi column is a tie. The README's non-SSE laptop column is an -O0 build (GLM 2375/7337 vs Eigen 8065/22404) and is not a meaningful comparison. The README says 1 million matrices times 10 repeats but src/Driver.cpp runs 10 matrices times 1,000,000 repeats. The Eigen test matrices set only the diagonal (off-diagonals not initialised in the generator). Compiler and NDK versions not stated, no repeats or variance. Second source (not used for the numbers): RasterDuck/vectormathbench intermediate-benchmarks.md (AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows, compiler not stated, 17 stars, GPL-3.0; BENCHMARKS.md there is empty) shows GLM ahead of DirectXMath on some vector composites (SSE4.2 ns/op: complex operation 1 1.51 vs 3.20, perspective matrix construction 2.20 vs 14.60) but behind on matrix-matrix multiply (22.13 vs 4.70) and model-matrix construction (160.76 vs 41.89); its README concludes Realtime Math and DirectXMath are generally faster than GLM. GLM's own test/perf programs only compare its scalar and SIMD paths and publish no numbers; the GLM README has no benchmark section.
